summary:
We developed Nasafarm, a Flutter-based agricultural decision-support app powered by an agri-intelligence backend. It combines NASA Earth observations, climate and soil datasets, regional crop knowledge, and farmer priorities to generate location-aware crop and rotation recommendations.

The platform enables farmers to manage fields, track seed and plant inventory, compare multi-year crop rotations, monitor environmental hazards, and explore recommendations with transparent scores, benefits, risks, and confidence levels. It integrates data from NASA POWER, Sentinel-2, MODIS, Landsat, SoilGrids, SRTM, and other environmental sources. AI-assisted analysis enhances recommendations while regional suitability rules ensure suggested crops match local climate and soil conditions.

Nasafarm addresses the challenge by connecting satellite observations and local agricultural information to practical farming decisions. Instead of offering generic crop suggestions, it compares rotation strategies according to water availability, soil health, erosion control, resilience, agronomic suitability, and market priorities.

Why it matters: Farmers need more than environmental data; they need understandable evidence to make better decisions. Nasafarm turns complex agricultural and satellite information into practical guidance, helping farmers explore more resilient and sustainable crop-rotation options while keeping local knowledge and farmer judgment central.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Nasafarm is an agricultural decision-support platform that connects satellite observations, environmental data, regional crop knowledge, and farmers’ priorities to help them make more informed crop-rotation decisions.

Farmers can add their fields, define their locations and characteristics, and analyze the environmental conditions affecting them. The backend gathers information from sources such as NASA POWER, GPM, Sentinel-2, MODIS, Landsat, SoilGrids, and SRTM, alongside climate information and soil characteristics.

The platform processes this information to build a regional environmental profile, assess crop suitability, and compare possible multi-year crop rotations. It evaluates factors such as water balance, soil health, erosion control, climate resilience, forage value, market considerations, and agronomic suitability. Farmers can compare proposed rotations, explore their benefits and risks, review confidence levels, and understand why a particular sequence is recommended.

Nasafarm also includes field management, seed and plant inventory, environmental hazard monitoring, AI-assisted analysis, and downloadable reports. Its recommendation system combines rule-based agricultural suitability checks with AI-assisted analysis, helping keep suggestions relevant to the region rather than relying on generic AI-generated crop lists.

What benefits does it have?

  • Better-informed decisions: Converts complex satellite, climate, and soil information into understandable agricultural insights.
  • Region-aware recommendations: Considers local environmental conditions and crop suitability instead of suggesting the same crops everywhere.
  • Improved crop-rotation planning: Helps farmers explore rotations that may support soil health, improve water management, reduce erosion, and strengthen resilience.
  • Greater transparency: Presents comparison scores, confidence levels, benefits, risks, and limitations rather than giving recommendations without explanation.
  • Environmental awareness: Provides field-related hazard alerts and historical environmental context.
  • Practical farm management: Brings field records, crop inventory, analysis, and reports together in one platform.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to help farmers move from reacting to environmental challenges toward making more informed, forward-looking decisions.

Crop rotation is not simply about choosing what to plant next. It involves understanding how crops interact with soil, water availability, weather patterns, and the previous seasons' agricultural decisions. Nasafarm aims to make this complexity more accessible by connecting Earth observation data with practical farming needs.

We want to support more resilient agricultural practices, encourage sustainable soil and water management, and make environmental information useful to farmers, particularly in regions where access to specialized agricultural analysis may be limited.

The platform is designed to support farmers and local agricultural expertise, not replace their judgment.

What tools and technologies did we use?

Mobile application

  • Flutter and Dart for the cross-platform mobile application.
  • Interactive maps and visual components for field management and presenting agricultural insights.

Backend and data processing

  • Python for the agricultural intelligence backend, data processing, suitability assessment, and recommendation logic.
  • HTTP APIs for communication between the application and backend.
  • JSON-based regional crop knowledge and suitability configuration.
  • Caching and persistence for managing analysis results and application data.

AI integration

  • Google Gemini API.
  • Groq API, using GPT-oss-120b.
  • AI-assisted analysis constrained by regional crop suitability information and environmental assessments.

Environmental and Earth observation data

  • NASA POWER for climate and meteorological information.
  • NASA GPM IMERG for precipitation observations.
  • SMAP for regional soil-moisture context.
  • Landsat, Sentinel-2, and MODIS for vegetation and Earth observation analysis.
  • SoilGrids for estimated soil properties.
  • SRTM for elevation and terrain information.
  • Open-Meteo and environmental hazard sources for additional weather and hazard context.

The project was developed primarily with Flutter, Dart, Python, and REST APIs, alongside mapping, geospatial, and data-processing tools.

How is the project creative?

The creative aspect of Nasafarm is not simply displaying satellite imagery or adding an AI chatbot to a farming application. It is connecting several different types of information into a practical agricultural decision-making process.

One important part of our work was addressing the problem of generic crop recommendations. We developed a regional crop knowledge system containing 56 crops and more than 149 crop names and aliases. Each crop has associated regional suitability, climate limits, and relevant agricultural characteristics. The recommendation engine uses this information to assess whether a crop is appropriate for a particular environment before presenting it as an option.

We also connect environmental analysis with multi-year crop-rotation planning. Instead of evaluating crops in isolation, Nasafarm considers how different crop sequences may affect agricultural priorities over time.

Another important design decision is making complex information understandable. We aim to present technical environmental indicators through comparisons, visual scores, field information, and clear explanations that farmers can actually use.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered several factors throughout development:

  • Local environmental conditions: Climate, rainfall, temperature extremes, soil properties, water availability, and terrain.
  • Regional crop suitability: Whether crops can realistically grow under the conditions of a particular location.
  • Long-term soil health: Crop sequences, nitrogen-related benefits, erosion control, and sustainable land management.
  • Water efficiency and resilience: Seasonal rainfall, dry periods, water stress, and changing environmental conditions.
  • Farmer priorities: Different farmers may prioritize market value, forage, water conservation, soil improvement, or resilience.
  • Data quality and uncertainty: Satellite products have different spatial and temporal resolutions, and regional estimates do not necessarily represent the exact conditions of an individual field. We therefore consider missing information, confidence, and the need for local validation.
  • Usability and accessibility: Agricultural recommendations should be understandable and practical, not buried under technical terminology.
  • Local knowledge: Farmers and agricultural specialists remain essential for validating recommendations and accounting for factors that remote sensing cannot fully capture.

Ultimately, Nasafarm aims to bridge the gap between the complexity of agricultural science and the everyday decisions farmers need to make. We want to turn Earth observation data into something more than maps and measurements: a practical tool for exploring better agricultural possibilities.
